articles.title: Thinking About Stopping Your GLP-1? What Happens to Your Weight, and How to Plan for It
articles.excerpt: Most people who stop semaglutide or tirzepatide regain some weight, but how much varies a lot. Here is what the research shows and how to plan the months after your last dose.
articles.seoTitle: Stopping a GLP-1: Weight Regain and How to Plan
articles.metaDescription: What happens when you stop semaglutide or tirzepatide? See what trials and real-world data show about weight regain, and how to build a maintenance plan.

content.text: People stop GLP-1 medications for all kinds of reasons. The cost goes up or insurance stops covering it. Side effects never fully settle. They hit their goal weight and want to see whether they still need it. Or they are planning a pregnancy. Whatever the reason, the question that comes up most is the same: will the weight come back?

content.alt: Three glass meal-prep containers filled with grains, lentils, corn, tomatoes, cucumber, and olives
content.caption: Planning meals ahead becomes more useful once appetite returns. Stock photo for illustration only; it does not show Harmony staff, patients, or a treatment result.

content.text: The honest answer is that some regain is likely, but the amount differs a great deal from person to person. A plan made before the last dose usually goes better than one made after the scale starts climbing.
What the clinical trials found

The clearest evidence comes from studies that stopped the medication on purpose and kept measuring. In the SURMOUNT-4 trial, published in JAMA, adults took tirzepatide for 36 weeks and lost an average of about 21% of their body weight. Half were then switched to a placebo without knowing it. Over the next year, that group regained an average of 14% of their body weight, while the group that stayed on tirzepatide lost another 5.5%.

Semaglutide showed a similar pattern. In an extension of the STEP 1 trial, people who stopped semaglutide regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost within a year. Blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol improvements mostly drifted back toward where they started, too.

A large review published in The BMJ in January 2026 pulled together 37 studies and more than 9,000 participants. People who had used semaglutide or tirzepatide regained roughly 10 kg (about 22 pounds) in the first year after stopping, and the researchers projected a return to starting weight after about a year and a half. Weight came back faster after stopping medication than after stopping a diet-and-exercise program alone.
Real-world results are more mixed

Trials report averages, and averages hide a lot. When Epic Research looked at health records for nearly 190,000 people who had stopped a GLP-1 after losing at least 5 pounds, about 56% of semaglutide users and 55% of tirzepatide users had kept their weight off or lost more two years later. Roughly one in five had regained all of it.

That kind of data has limits. It cannot show why people stopped, whether some restarted later, or what else changed in their lives. Still, it is a useful reminder that regain is common but not automatic, and that what happens next is partly within your control.
Why the weight tends to return

GLP-1 medications quiet hunger and help you feel full sooner. When the medication wears off, those signals usually come back, sometimes stronger than people expect. At the same time, the body responds to weight loss by burning slightly less energy and pushing appetite up. None of this is a lack of willpower. It is biology, and it is the reason many specialists now treat obesity as a long-term condition rather than a problem that is solved once.
Before your last dose: questions to settle with your provider

Is stopping the right move, or would a lower maintenance dose make more sense for me?
Should I stop all at once or step the dose down over a few weeks?
Do any of my other medications, such as diabetes or blood pressure medications, need to change when this one stops?
What weight change should prompt me to call you?
If I am planning a pregnancy, how far ahead do I need to stop? (The Wegovy prescribing information, for example, says to stop at least two months before a planned pregnancy.)

On tapering: there is not yet good trial evidence that stepping down slowly prevents regain. Some clinicians still prefer it because it lets appetite return gradually and gives you time to adjust. It is a reasonable conversation to have, but it is not a guarantee.
A maintenance plan that holds up
The habits that matter most after stopping are the same ones that protect your results while you are still on medication. Starting them early gives you a head start.

Protein at every meal. It helps with fullness and protects muscle. Many clinicians suggest roughly 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight per day for adults managing weight, adjusted for kidney health and other conditions.
Strength training two to three times a week. Muscle you keep now makes maintenance easier later.
A regular weigh-in. Once a week, same day, same time, is enough to spot a trend without obsessing over daily swings.
A clear trigger point. Decide in advance that a gain of a set amount, often around 5 pounds, means a check-in with your provider rather than waiting until it becomes 20.
Sleep and alcohol. Short sleep and regular drinking both make appetite harder to manage, and they tend to creep back in over the holidays.
Structure for the first three months. This is when hunger usually returns most noticeably, so planned meals and snacks help more than relying on how you feel in the moment.
If the weight starts coming back

Regain is not a failure, and it is not a reason to avoid your provider. Some people do well with a lower dose taken long term. Others restart for a period, and some move to a different medication if cost or side effects were the problem. The earlier you raise it, the more options you usually have.
How Harmony Med Spa can help

Harmony's medical weight-loss program in Sarasota includes a practitioner consultation, a personalized plan, and ongoing follow-up visits. If you are thinking about stopping, or you already have, book a visit before your last dose if you can. Bring your current weight, your dose history, and a list of your other medications, and we can build a maintenance plan around your goals and budget.

items.question: Will I definitely regain weight if I stop my GLP-1?
items.answer: Not necessarily, but some regain is common. Trials show most people regain a large share within a year on average, while real-world records suggest about half keep most of their loss for two years.

items.question: How fast does weight come back after stopping semaglutide or tirzepatide?
items.answer: In a 2026 BMJ review, people regained about 22 pounds in the first year on average, with a projected return to starting weight in roughly a year and a half. Individual results vary widely.

items.question: Is it better to taper off a GLP-1?
items.answer: There is no strong trial evidence that tapering prevents regain. Some providers taper to let appetite return gradually. Ask your provider which approach fits your situation.

items.question: Can I stop my GLP-1 once I reach my goal weight?
items.answer: You can, but plan for it. Many people do better with a maintenance strategy, which might include a lower dose, closer follow-up, or a clear plan for restarting if weight returns.

items.question: What habits help most after stopping?
items.answer: Enough protein, regular strength training, weekly weigh-ins, good sleep, limited alcohol, and a preset weight gain that triggers a check-in with your provider.

items.question: Do I need to stop a GLP-1 before getting pregnant?
items.answer: Yes, with planning. The Wegovy label advises stopping at least two months before a planned pregnancy. Talk with your provider about timing for your specific medication.

articles.title: Under-Eye Filler: Who It Helps, Who Should Skip It, and What Changed in 2026
articles.excerpt: Under-eye filler can soften a hollow, tired look, but it is the wrong fix for puffiness and most dark circles. Here is how to tell the difference before you book.
articles.seoTitle: Under-Eye Filler: Good Candidates and Risks
articles.metaDescription: Tear trough filler can soften under-eye hollows, but not puffiness or pigment. Learn who is a good candidate, the risks, and the new FDA-approved options.

content.text: "I look tired even when I'm not" is one of the most common things people say in an injectables consultation. Sometimes under-eye filler is a good answer to that. Often it isn't. The under-eye area is small, the skin is thin, and the reasons it looks dark or hollow vary a lot from one face to the next. Getting the cause right matters more here than almost anywhere else on the face.

content.alt: Close-up of an adult woman's eye and lower lid showing the under-eye area and fine lines
content.caption: Hollowing, puffiness, pigment, and crepey texture can look similar at a glance but call for different treatments. Stock photo for illustration only; it does not show Harmony staff, patients, or a treatment result.

content.text: Hollows, puffiness, and dark circles are different problems

Filler adds volume. It works best when the main issue is a groove or hollow below the eye that catches shadow, often called the tear trough. It does not fix problems caused by something else, and in some cases it can make them look worse.

Hollowness: a visible groove or sunken look under the eye, usually from volume loss with age, genetics, or weight loss. This is what under-eye filler is designed for.
Puffiness or bags: fat that pushes forward under the lower lid, or fluid that comes and goes. Adding filler on top can make bags bigger.
Festoons: swelling that sits lower, on the upper cheek. Filler can make these worse, and they usually need a different approach.
Pigment: brown or purple coloring in the skin itself. Filler will not change skin color.
Crepey texture: fine, wrinkled skin. This usually responds better to skin treatments than to volume.

A quick self-check: stand under an overhead light and look straight into a mirror. If the darkness changes a lot as you tilt your head back or turn toward the light, shadow from a hollow may be part of it. If the color stays the same in every light, pigment is more likely.
What changed in 2026

For years, much of the under-eye filler done in the U.S. was off-label, meaning the products were approved for other areas of the face. That has been changing. Juvéderm Volbella XC was the first hyaluronic acid filler approved by the FDA for under-eye hollows, followed by Restylane Eyelight in 2023. In August 2026, the FDA approved RHA Redensity Eye, from the RHA line made by Teoxane and distributed by Revance, for moderate to severe under-eye hollowing in adults 22 and older.

In its 52-week trial, 93% of people treated showed improvement at three months, according to the companies. Independent experts have pointed out that a trial of that size and length cannot rule out rare complications or problems that show up years later. That is true of every filler in this area, and it is why technique and patient selection still matter more than the name on the syringe.
At your consultation, it is fair to ask which product your injector plans to use, whether it is approved for the under-eye area, and why they chose it for you.
Who tends to be a good candidate

Adults with a visible hollow or groove under the eye and relatively good skin quality
Little or no puffiness or bagging in the lower lid
Realistic goals, such as looking more rested rather than completely erasing the area
No active infection, eye inflammation, or recent eye surgery
A willingness to start with a small amount and reassess

Sometimes the best under-eye result starts somewhere else. When the cheek has lost volume, the under-eye area can look hollower than it really is. Supporting the cheek first may soften the area with less product placed directly under the eye.
Who should probably skip it

Under-eye filler is usually not the right choice if your main concern is puffiness, bags, festoons, or dark pigment. People with very thin, loose lower-lid skin may also see the product, or develop a bluish tint known as the Tyndall effect. If you have a history of allergies that cause swelling around the eyes, mention it, because recurring puffiness can be worse after filler. For significant bags or loose skin, a surgical consultation for a lower blepharoplasty may make more sense.
Risks to understand

Bruising and swelling are the most common side effects and usually settle within a week or so. Less common problems include lumps, visible product, ongoing puffiness, and filler moving out of place, and some of these can appear months later. The most serious risk with any filler is accidental injection into a blood vessel. The FDA notes it is uncommon but can cause tissue damage and, rarely, vision loss or blindness. The area around the eyes needs particular care because of the vessels nearby.
One advantage of hyaluronic acid fillers is that they can usually be dissolved with an enzyme called hyaluronidase if there is a problem or you dislike the result.
Seek care right away if you notice vision changes, severe or worsening pain, or skin that turns white, gray, or dusky after treatment.
If filler is not the answer

For crepey texture and fine lines: RF microneedling or fractional CO2 laser, depending on skin type and downtime
For pigment: sun protection, medical-grade skincare, and, for some skin types, light-based treatment
For volume loss in the mid-face: cheek filler or a collagen stimulator such as Sculptra
For bags and puffiness: a look at allergies, sleep, and salt, and for persistent bags, a surgical opinion
Under-eye filler at Harmony Med Spa

Harmony offers dermal fillers for under-eye hollows in Sarasota, along with RHA and other hyaluronic acid fillers for the cheeks, lips, and lines. Filler is priced at $714 per full syringe or $382.50 per half syringe, and the under-eye area often needs a modest amount. Your injector will look at your whole face in different lighting before recommending anything, and if filler is not the right tool, we will tell you and talk through what else might help.

items.question: Does under-eye filler get rid of dark circles?
items.answer: Only when the darkness is mostly shadow from a hollow. Filler does not change brown or purple pigment in the skin.

items.question: Is under-eye filler FDA approved?
items.answer: Some products are. Juvéderm Volbella XC, Restylane Eyelight, and, since August 2026, RHA Redensity Eye are FDA approved for under-eye hollows in adults. Ask which product your injector plans to use.

items.question: How long does tear trough filler last?
items.answer: It varies by product and person. Many results last around a year, and some longer. In the RHA Redensity Eye trial, some people kept results up to 12 months without a touch-up.

items.question: Can under-eye filler make bags worse?
items.answer: Yes. If puffiness comes from fat or fluid, adding volume can make the area look fuller. That is why the consultation matters.

items.question: What is the Tyndall effect?
items.answer: A bluish tint that can appear when hyaluronic acid filler sits too close to the surface in thin skin. It can usually be corrected by dissolving the filler.

items.question: Can under-eye filler be reversed?
items.answer: Hyaluronic acid filler can usually be dissolved with hyaluronidase, which is one reason it is the preferred type of filler for this area.

articles.title: Your First Lip Filler: Half Syringe or Full, the Swelling Timeline, and Keeping It Natural
articles.excerpt: A first lip filler appointment goes better when you know what a half syringe can do, how long swelling lasts, and when to judge the result. Here is the practical version.
articles.seoTitle: First Lip Filler: Half vs. Full Syringe Guide
articles.metaDescription: Getting lip filler for the first time? Learn how a half and full syringe compare, what swelling looks like day by day, aftercare, and warning signs.

content.text: Most first-time lip filler patients have the same worry, and it is not the needle. It is ending up with lips that look obviously "done." The good news is that a natural result is mostly about planning: choosing the right amount, placing it where your lips actually need it, and giving the swelling time to settle before you decide how it looks.

content.alt: Injector in pink gloves placing hyaluronic acid filler in a young woman's lower lip while she reclines
content.caption: Stock photo for illustration only; it does not show Harmony staff, patients, or a treatment result.

content.text: Start with what you want to change
"Bigger" is only one of the things lip filler can do, and often it is not the main goal. Before your appointment, think about which of these matters most to you:

Definition: a crisper lip border or a more visible cupid's bow
Hydration and smoothness: softer texture without much change in size
Balance: evening out an upper and lower lip that do not match, or one side that is fuller
Volume: more fullness overall
Lines around the mouth: softening vertical lines above the upper lip

Bring a photo of your own lips from a few years ago if you liked them better then. Photos of other people can help with direction, but your lip shape, teeth, and facial proportions will shape what looks natural on you.
Half syringe or full syringe?

A typical syringe of hyaluronic acid filler holds about 1 mL. At Harmony, filler is $714 per full syringe or $382.50 per half syringe. For many first-timers, a half syringe gives a visible but subtle change, especially when the goal is definition or balance. A full syringe gives more room to add volume or treat both lips and the border in one visit.

Many injectors suggest starting on the conservative side. Filler can be added at a follow-up once you have lived with the result for a few weeks. Taking it away means dissolving it, which is possible but less pleasant. If your budget allows a full syringe but your injector recommends half, that is usually a good sign.
Before your appointment

If you get cold sores, tell your injector. Lip injections can trigger an outbreak, and you may be prescribed an antiviral to take beforehand.
Book at least two weeks before a wedding, photos, or a big event, so swelling and any bruising have time to settle.
Skip alcohol the night before, since it can make bruising more likely.
Do not stop any prescribed blood thinner or aspirin on your own. Tell your injector what you take and ask your prescribing provider if a change is safe.
Mention any dental work coming up. Many injectors prefer a gap of about two weeks before or after.
What the appointment is like

Most hyaluronic acid lip fillers contain lidocaine, a numbing medicine, and many injectors also use a numbing cream first. Expect pressure and some stinging rather than sharp pain. The injecting itself usually takes 15 to 30 minutes, with time before and after for photos, planning, and a final check. Your lips will look fuller right away, but that first look includes swelling.
The swelling timeline

Day 1: noticeable swelling, often uneven. Lips can feel firm or lumpy.
Days 2 to 3: swelling often peaks. This is the day people panic, and it is almost never the final look.
Days 4 to 7: most of the swelling goes down. Small bruises fade.
Around 2 weeks: the filler has settled. This is the time to judge the result and to book a touch-up if you want one.
A cold compress for short periods and sleeping with your head slightly raised for the first night or two can help with swelling.
Aftercare basics

Avoid strenuous exercise for about 24 hours
Skip lipstick and lip products for the first day unless your injector says otherwise
Do not press, massage, or pinch the lips unless you were told to
Avoid very hot drinks and saunas for a day or two
Hold off on dental cleanings for about two weeks
When to call right away

Serious complications are uncommon, but you should know the signs. Accidental injection into a blood vessel is the most concerning risk with any filler. Call your injector immediately, or seek urgent care, if you notice skin on or around the lips turning white, gray, blue, or dusky, pain that is severe or getting worse instead of better, or any change in your vision. Fast treatment matters.
Also call if you develop a fever, increasing redness, or a lump that becomes hot and painful in the days or weeks after treatment.
A note on needle-free filler pens

You may see "hyaluron pens" sold online or offered at parties. The FDA has warned the public not to use needle-free devices to inject lip or facial fillers. These devices use high pressure, give little control over where the filler goes, and are often paired with fillers that are not FDA approved.
How long it lasts, and how to reverse it

Lip filler often lasts around six months to a year. Lips move constantly, so filler there tends to break down faster than in the cheeks. Some people keep a result longer. Because hyaluronic acid filler can usually be dissolved with an enzyme called hyaluronidase, a result you do not like is not permanent.
Lip filler at Harmony Med Spa

Harmony's injectors in Sarasota start every lip treatment with a conversation about your goals and proportions, then build a plan that can grow over time. If you are unsure about size, start with a half syringe and come back once it settles. Qualifying RHA filler treatments can also earn REVA Rewards.

items.question: Is half a syringe of lip filler enough?
items.answer: For many first-timers, yes. A half syringe usually gives a subtle change in shape or definition. You can add more after the filler settles.

items.question: How long does lip filler swelling last?
items.answer: Swelling usually peaks around day two or three and mostly fades within a week. Allow about two weeks before judging the final result.

items.question: Does lip filler hurt?
items.answer: Most people feel pressure and stinging rather than sharp pain. Many fillers contain lidocaine, and numbing cream is often used first.

items.question: How long does lip filler last?
items.answer: Often six months to a year, though it varies. Lips move a lot, so filler there may break down faster than in other areas.

items.question: Can lip filler be dissolved?
items.answer: Hyaluronic acid filler can usually be dissolved with an enzyme called hyaluronidase if there is a problem or you dislike the result.

items.answer: Filler is $714 per full syringe or $382.50 per half syringe. Your injector will recommend an amount at your consultation.

articles.title: What Menopause Does to Your Skin, and Which Treatments Actually Help
articles.excerpt: Skin can lose close to a third of its collagen in the first five years after menopause. Here is what changes, what you can do at home, and which in-office treatments fit each concern.
articles.seoTitle: Menopause Skin Changes: What Helps and Why
articles.metaDescription: Menopause brings dryness, thinner skin, and faster collagen loss. Learn why it happens and how skincare, hormone therapy, and in-office treatments can help.

content.text: Plenty of women notice their skin change before they connect it to menopause. Moisturizer that used to be enough suddenly isn't. Makeup settles into lines that weren't there last year. Breakouts show up in your 50s. Skin bruises more easily and takes longer to heal. These changes are common, they have a clear biological cause, and there is more you can do about them than most people are told.

content.alt: Smiling woman in her sixties applying moisturizer to her cheek outdoors
content.caption: Stock photo for illustration only; it does not show Harmony staff, patients, or a treatment result.

content.text: Why skin changes so quickly after menopause

Estrogen helps skin hold on to collagen, water, and oil. When estrogen drops, skin loses those things faster. A review in Clinical and Experimental Dermatology describes a rapid fall in skin collagen after menopause, with close to a third lost in the first five years and about 2% a year after that. The authors note that collagen loss tracks the number of years since menopause more closely than chronological age.
Lower estrogen also weakens the skin barrier, so more water escapes through the surface. That is a big part of why skin that was fine for decades can start to feel tight, itchy, or easily irritated.
The most common changes

Dryness and itching, especially on the arms, legs, and face
Thinner skin that bruises more easily
Loss of firmness and new sagging along the jawline and neck
Fine lines that deepen faster than before
Brown spots from years of sun showing up more clearly
Adult acne, sometimes for the first time
Coarse hairs on the chin, jaw, or upper lip
Slower healing after scratches, procedures, or irritation
What helps at home
The American Academy of Dermatology's advice for menopausal skin is refreshingly simple, and most of it costs very little.

Wash with a mild, fragrance-free cleanser instead of soap
Moisturize right after bathing and again whenever skin feels dry
Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher every day, which matters even more in Sarasota
Consider a product with retinol or peptides for lines and firmness, introduced slowly
Check with a skin professional before scrubbing, at-home peels, or microdermabrasion, which can do more harm to thinner skin
Get new or changing spots checked, since skin cancer risk rises with age and sun exposure
If your skin has become reactive, simplify first. A short routine of cleanser, moisturizer, and sunscreen for a few weeks often calms things down before you add active ingredients back in.
Where hormone therapy fits

Studies have found that estrogen therapy can raise skin collagen and thickness, sometimes within a few months. That is real, but it is not a reason to start hormone therapy on its own. Hormone therapy is prescribed for menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and sleep problems, after weighing your personal health history and risks. If you are already considering it for those reasons, better skin may be a welcome side benefit. It is not a replacement for sunscreen or skin treatments, and it can cause skin side effects of its own in some people, such as acne or unwanted hair growth.
Matching in-office treatments to the problem
No single treatment covers every menopause skin change. The better approach is to pick the concern that bothers you most and start there.

Loss of firmness and crepey texture: RF microneedling, which uses tiny needles and heat to prompt new collagen, usually as a series
Gradual loss of facial volume: Sculptra, a collagen stimulator that works over several months, or hyaluronic acid filler for targeted areas
Deeper lines and rough texture: fractional CO2 laser, which offers more change with more downtime
Brown spots and redness: IPL photofacial, for suitable skin types
Dullness and dryness: medical-grade facials and a skincare plan built around barrier repair
Unwanted dark facial hair: laser hair removal, which works on pigmented hair but not on gray, white, or very light hair

Because healing can be slower after menopause, providers often use more conservative settings, allow more time between sessions, and spend more time on preparation and aftercare. That is normal, and it usually gives a better result than rushing.
When to see a doctor first

Some skin changes need a medical look before any cosmetic treatment. See a dermatologist or your primary care provider for a mole or spot that is new, changing, bleeding, or not healing; itching that keeps you up at night or comes with a rash; or sudden, rapid hair growth, which can have causes other than menopause.
How Harmony Med Spa can help

At Harmony, you can talk about menopause symptoms and skin with the same team. Our providers offer hormone evaluations and bioidentical hormone replacement therapy for eligible patients, alongside RF microneedling, Sculptra, fillers, CO2 and IPL treatments, medical-grade facials, and skincare. Start with a consultation, bring a list of your current products and medications, and we will help you decide what to do first.

items.question: Why is my skin so dry after menopause?
items.answer: Lower estrogen weakens the skin barrier and reduces oil and water in the skin, so moisture escapes faster. Gentle cleansers, regular moisturizer, and fewer harsh products usually help.

items.question: How much collagen do you lose after menopause?
items.answer: Research suggests close to a third of skin collagen is lost in the first five years after menopause, then about 2% a year for the next 15 years.

items.question: Does hormone therapy improve skin?
items.answer: Estrogen therapy has been shown to increase skin collagen and thickness, but it is prescribed for menopause symptoms, not for skin alone. The decision depends on your health history and risks.

items.question: What is the best treatment for sagging skin after menopause?
items.answer: It depends on how much laxity you have. RF microneedling and Sculptra can help mild to moderate loss of firmness. Significant sagging may need a surgical opinion.

items.question: Can I still have laser treatments after menopause?
items.answer: Usually yes. Providers may use gentler settings and more recovery time because skin heals more slowly. Tell your provider about any medications you take.

items.question: Why am I getting acne in my 50s?
items.answer: Shifts in the balance of hormones can trigger breakouts during and after menopause. Use non-drying products, and see a dermatologist if it does not improve.

articles.title: Loose Skin and Dull Texture After GLP-1 Weight Loss: What Helps, and When to Start
articles.primaryKeyword: skin changes after GLP-1 weight loss
articles.excerpt: Fast weight loss can leave skin looking looser and more tired than you expected. Here is what is actually happening, which treatments fit which change, and why timing matters.
articles.seoTitle: Skin Changes After GLP-1 Weight Loss: What Helps
articles.metaDescription: Loose skin or a tired look after GLP-1 weight loss? Learn what causes it, when to start treatment, and how RF microneedling, Sculptra, and filler compare.
articles.ctaLabel: Plan skin treatment around your weight loss

content.text: Losing a significant amount of weight on semaglutide or tirzepatide can change how you feel in a matter of months. Your skin does not always keep up. Some people notice a hollow or tired look in the face. Others see looser skin along the jaw, neck, arms, or stomach, or skin that just looks duller than it used to. The internet calls the facial version "Ozempic face." It is a catchy name, but it gets the cause slightly wrong, and that matters when you are choosing a treatment.

content.text: It is the weight loss, not a direct effect of the drug

There is no good evidence that GLP-1 medications damage skin directly. As one King's College London dermatologist put it to Reuters in October 2026, "The drug doesn't melt your collagen." What changes is the fat underneath. The face has fat pads that give it shape and support, and when they shrink quickly, skin that has lost some elasticity with age and sun cannot always tighten to match. The same thing happens after any large or fast weight loss, with or without medication.

That explains why the changes tend to be more noticeable in people who lose more weight, lose it quickly, or are older. Low protein intake during weight loss can make things look worse, too, because it affects muscle, skin, and hair.
The industry has noticed

Skincare and aesthetics companies now see GLP-1 users as a major market. Galderma, which makes Sculptra and Restylane, has studied how its existing treatments perform on GLP-1-related skin changes, and L'Oréal says it is testing products on GLP-1 users. None of these treatments is approved specifically for GLP-1 users, and experts are clear that creams cannot reach or replace the deep fat pads of the face. Topical products can improve how skin looks and feels on the surface. They cannot rebuild lost volume.
Timing: why waiting usually pays off

If you are still losing weight steadily, your face and body will keep changing. Treating volume loss too early can mean paying for results that look different a few months later. Many providers suggest waiting until your weight has been fairly stable for a few months before committing to volume treatments such as filler or Sculptra.
That does not mean doing nothing. Some things are worth starting right away:

Protein and strength training to protect muscle, which supports the face and body underneath the skin
Daily SPF 30 or higher, since sun damage makes skin less able to bounce back
A simple skincare routine with a retinoid at night, if your skin tolerates it, and a good moisturizer
Skin-quality treatments such as RF microneedling, which can begin while you are still losing weight and build collagen over time
Matching the treatment to the change

Mild looseness and crepey texture on the face or neck: RF microneedling, usually as a series spaced several weeks apart
Gradual loss of fullness across the cheeks and temples: Sculptra, which stimulates collagen over several months and suits people who want a slow, subtle change
A specific hollow, such as under the cheekbone or at the temple: hyaluronic acid filler for a more immediate, targeted result
Rough texture, enlarged pores, or deeper lines: fractional CO2 laser, with more downtime and more change
Loose skin on the body: RF microneedling can help mild laxity in some areas, but expectations should be modest

Most people get the best result from a combination over time rather than one big appointment, for example a series of RF microneedling to improve skin quality, followed by Sculptra or filler once weight has settled.
Knowing the limits

Non-surgical treatments work best for mild to moderate change. If you have a large amount of loose skin, especially on the neck, abdomen, or arms after major weight loss, energy-based devices and injectables will not remove it. In that case, a consultation with a board-certified plastic surgeon is the honest next step, and a good med spa should tell you so.

items.question: Do GLP-1 medications cause loose skin?
items.answer: Not directly. Loose skin and facial hollowing come from losing fat quickly, especially when skin has lost elasticity with age or sun. The same can happen after any large weight loss.

items.question: What is Ozempic face?
items.answer: A popular term for a hollow or aged look in the face after rapid weight loss on GLP-1 medications. Dermatologists note the cause is fat loss, not the drug damaging collagen.

items.question: When should I start treating skin after GLP-1 weight loss?
items.answer: Skin-quality treatments like RF microneedling can start anytime. Many providers suggest waiting until weight has been stable for a few months before volume treatments like filler or Sculptra.

items.question: Can creams fix GLP-1 face?
items.answer: Skincare can improve surface texture and hydration, but it cannot replace the deep facial fat that was lost.

items.question: Does RF microneedling tighten skin after weight loss?
items.answer: It can improve mild laxity and texture by stimulating collagen over several months. It will not remove large amounts of loose skin.

items.question: Should I choose Sculptra or filler after weight loss?
items.answer: Sculptra builds collagen gradually for broad, subtle volume. Filler gives immediate, targeted volume. Many people use both at different stages.
